A research programme pairing professional mediators and negotiation scholars with cooperative-AI researchers would turn concepts such as ripeness, face-saving and third-party mediation into tests of how AI agents escalate and settle conflicts.
gaps.detail: Multi-agent AI is the least-covered problem on the whole map (34 entries, 14 primary), and the discovery notes say peace-and-conflict researchers and mediators are absent from AI–AI conflict, with CLR almost alone. Cooperative-AI groups on the map (FOCAL (CMU), Witt Lab, Modeling Cooperation, Equilibria Network) and the Concordia simulation library work mostly from game theory and computer science. Practitioner knowledge sits in GCSP (its PIN negotiation programme, not yet applied to AI), CMI and HD AI & Emerging Tech. The democracy notes add a second gap: no one systematically red-teams AI mediators (Habermas Machine is dormant). Success would be an open evaluation suite that tests whether LLM agents recognise deadlock, take face-saving exits, accept a mediator's single negotiating text, or escalate, developed by mixed teams of mediators and researchers. Risks: mediators' skill is largely tacit and may not translate. Better negotiating agents are also a capability, so evaluations should measure escalation and failure to settle rather than train agents to win.
steps: Run a two-day workshop pairing PIN, CMI and HD practitioners with researchers from FOCAL, Witt Lab and the Concordia team to choose five concepts from mediation practice that can be tested in agents.
Fund three or four mediator–researcher pairs to build scenarios in the Concordia library, published as an open evaluation suite.

Approach multi-agent funders (Macroscopic Ventures, Schmidt Sciences, and the Cooperative AI Foundation, which is not on the map) to co-fund, and use findings on AI escalation in wargames as a second test bed.
gaps.evidence: Peace × Multi-agent is one of four empty peace problem cells. multi-agent AI has 34 entries in total (14 primary), the fewest of any problem. None of the 51 peace entries transfers knowledge into the model. The neuro discovery notes say mediation and diplomacy practitioners are absent from AI–AI conflict. GCSP's profile says the link from PIN to AI agreements is a possibility, not current work.

gaps.title: Competition economists and regulators as monitors of AI agent markets
gaps.summary: IO economists and competition authorities have the deepest evidence that AI agents collude without being told to. Yet only 2 of 56 economics organisations tag multi-agent AI, and the map has no competition authority or market-design group. A small lab or working group pairing them with cooperative-AI researchers would build a shared testbed and a monitoring practice for agent economies.
gaps.detail: Experiments show LLM pricing agents reaching supracompetitive prices on their own, with the effect sensitive to wording in the prompt (Fish, Gonczarowski and Shorrer, 2024, presented at the AEA in 2025). Sellers handing pricing to the same few models adds correlation without any communication between them. Agent payment protocols are being built by companies, not by auction theorists or safety researchers. Nearby on the map: FOCAL (CMU), Teesside AI race models, Normativity Lab, the multi-agent crisis argument of LSE Systemic Risk Centre, Protocol Labs (economic infrastructure for agents) and the behavioural experiments of CHM (MPIB Berlin). CAIF, which is on the aisafety.com map but not profiled here, funds multi-agent work and must be checked first. Success would be an open testbed of LLM agents in pricing, auction and procurement markets, detection methods co-written with competition-authority technologists, and collusion established as a standard multi-agent safety evaluation. The risks: it could shrink into ordinary antitrust with no safety relevance, competition authorities have little spare capacity, and CAIF's 2026 grants may already cover parts of it.
steps: Check CAIF's 2026 grant awards and the multi-agent risks literature, so the work does not duplicate what they fund.

Convene IO economists working on algorithmic collusion, technologists from the CMA, DG COMP and the Bundeskartellamt, and multi-agent safety researchers at a workshop beside an economics-and-computation or NeurIPS meeting.
Fund an open agent-market testbed and a two-year postdoc pair: one IO economist and one multi-agent RL researcher.
Add competition authorities and market-design labs to the map's potential ring.
gaps.evidence: Economics × Multi-agent: 2 of 56 (Protocol Labs, LSE Systemic Risk Centre). Economics × Agency: empty. The map has no competition authority. Multi-agent is tagged by only 34 organisations across the whole map. The discovery notes list algorithmic collusion and agent-economy design as missing bridges.

gaps.title: Safety science for open-ended AI, built with the artificial-life community
gaps.summary: Frontier labs now pursue open-ended, self-improving systems, an idea artificial life has studied for three decades. Yet no organisation owns the safety of open-ended search, and the field's learned society has no AI-safety track. A standing workshop at ALIFE 2027 in Prague, co-run with ACS, followed by a small research group, would bring that knowledge across.
gaps.detail: ISAL is tagged as having no AI work at all, even though its field holds the deepest knowledge of open-ended evolution: novelty measures, major transitions, and how evolving populations escape their designers' intentions. On the ML side the topic exists only as papers: Ecoffet, Clune and Lehman (2020), a 2025 ICLR workshop paper arguing that safety is essential for open-ended systems, and a 2026 ICML position paper from CISPA. None of these is a programme, and none draws on ALife's community. NOOMA Labs (Kyoto) argues in PNAS Nexus that a diverse ecosystem of AI agents is a safer target than full alignment, and Japan's ALIGN draws on ALife, so the intellectual seeds are there. Success would be a recurring ALIFE workshop, a shared benchmark for open-ended search that stays within agreed bounds, and a three-to-five-person group whose alumni move into labs and safety institutes. The main risk is that safety-of-open-endedness work slides into capability work, since open-endedness is itself a frontier capability agenda. The ALife community may also resist x-risk framing.
steps: Approach the ALIFE 2027 organisers (Prague, 19-23 July 2027) together with ACS Research at Charles University, Prague, to propose a workshop on the safety of open-ended systems.
Commission a short review mapping what artificial life knows about steering and bounding open-ended evolution onto current lab agendas (self-improving agents, automated-scientist systems).
Fund two or three ALife researchers through an explicit open-endedness stream of the PIBBSS fellowship run by Principles of Intelligence.
If the workshop draws well, seed a small group at NOOMA Labs or as a Prague node alongside ACS.
gaps.evidence: ISAL is tagged transfer no AI work yet. The biology discovery notes state that 'no organisation owns its safety'. biology & diverse intelligence has 8 potential entries but only 1 core (Softmax). A quick web search found ML-side position papers (ICLR 2025 workshop, ICML 2026) but no organisation or ALife-side programme.

gaps.title: A social choice programme for aggregating public input into AI specifications
gaps.summary: No formal-rooted organisation on the map works on democratic voice: Formal × Democracy is empty, and only two formal entries address what AI should value. A standing programme would put social choice theorists to work on how labs and deliberation projects turn conflicting public input into model specifications and constitutions.
gaps.detail: Social choice theory has decades of results on aggregating conflicting preferences, from impossibility theorems to proportional rules. The relevant people are on the map but not connected: Christian List at MCMP (LMU), Jobst Heitzig's social-choice and agency-preserving work at PIK BeGa (Heitzig), Conitzer's FOCAL (CMU), and Topos's co-specification tools (Topos Institute). The deliberation organisations that already feed models (CIP, CompDem (Polis), MAI) are rooted in democracy or philosophy, not formal theory. Academic interest exists: the ICML 2026 Pluralistic Alignment workshop, a June 2026 survey on alignment from social choice perspectives, and the PlurVA-LLM workshop in November 2026. But nothing sustains it between conferences, and ARIA's pages no longer mention the deliberative-specification strand of Safeguarded AI (inferred, not confirmed). Success would be a group of three to five researchers paired with one deliberation organisation, publishing aggregation rules with stated guarantees (what minorities are assured of, where strategic manipulation is possible) that a lab or an AI safety institute adopts. Risks: lab-internal 'collective alignment' teams may already crowd the space, the theory may produce impossibility results that practitioners ignore, and some of this work may already be filed under the democracy tradition.
steps: int/a convenes a two-day working session pairing List (MCMP), Heitzig (PIK) and Conitzer's group with CIP, CompDem and MAI, all working on one concrete question: how a specific published public-input process should aggregate its results.
A funder offers a two-year pilot (two postdocs) at MCMP or PIK, on condition that a deliberation partner co-designs the problem.
Ask ARIA whether Safeguarded AI's sociotechnical specification strand has been dropped; if it has, offer Topos Institute a bridge grant to adapt CatColab for stakeholders to specify jointly.
List the authors of the 2026 social-choice-and-alignment papers and check which of them have institutional backing beyond a single paper.
gaps.evidence: Formal × Democracy is an empty cell. Formal × Values has only two entries (CORAL, PIK BeGa (Heitzig)). Topos Institute is the only formal-home organisation with democracy as a secondary tradition, and it is tagged assurance and epistemics. The discovery notes say ARIA's current page no longer mentions deliberative specification work.

gaps.title: World Wide Views-style Global or distributed deliberation on frontier-AI risk before May 2027
gaps.summary: The UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance has a Citizens' Track that invites decentralised citizen assemblies to feed the second Dialogue (New York, 3-4 May 2027). Nothing ensures that frontier-AI thresholds or loss-of-control questions reach those agendas, or that the results can be compared across countries. Funding a synchronised deliberation in 30 or more countries on a single protocol, built on the Danish Board of Technology's World Wide Views method, would fill this.
gaps.detail: The method already exists in this tradition. Democracy X (potential ring; formerly the Danish Board of Technology) ran World Wide Views on climate and biodiversity in dozens of countries at once. Missions Publiques, behind Global AI Dialogue (unverified, no results since Feb 2025), ran the 'We, the Internet' Global or distributed dialogue. Odyssean has an AI governance assembly proposal, and CIP's Global Dialogues are surveys, not deliberation. Connected by Data published design options for Global or distributed citizen deliberation on AI in Sept 2024, and it and Ada pushed for the Citizens' Track. Success would be a comparable cross-national verdict on questions such as pause conditions, capability thresholds and who should decide, presented in May 2027. The risks: seven months is tight; cost is probably in the millions (I have not checked a budget); governments may ignore the results; and x-risk questions framed carelessly will look like advocacy, so briefing materials must be reviewed by both safety and ethics experts. I have not checked how the Citizens' Track is run beyond its published description.
steps: Contact the Citizens' Track organisers to learn the 2027 agenda, the submission format and whether frontier-risk questions are in scope.
Convene Democracy X, Missions Publiques, Odyssean, DemocracyNext and CIP to agree a common protocol and question set. int/a's Paris hub is close to Missions Publiques and Make.org and could host.
Fund national host partners, with deliberate inclusion of Africa and Latin America through People Powered's member network.
Commission balanced briefing materials, peer-reviewed from both the AI-safety and AI-ethics sides.
gaps.evidence: Only 6 of 69 entries use a catastrophic or existential framing. Core has just 2 deliberation entries (Odyssean Institute, AI & Democracy Fdn). Global AI Dialogue is 'unverified', and Democracy X is 'potential' with light AI engagement. There are zero Africa or Latin America entries in the tradition. The collective angle's missing bridge 2 says frontier questions are rarely put to representative publics. A web check confirmed the Citizens' Track and the May 2027 date.

gaps.title: Citizens' consensus conference on AI moral status and welfare
gaps.summary: Policy on whether AI systems might matter morally is being shaped by labs and a few philosophers, while the public is only polled; I found no citizens' deliberation on AI moral status anywhere. A consensus conference, run by a practitioner that has just held one on animal welfare, would show what informed publics conclude and give welfare policy a basis in legitimacy.
gaps.detail: The Democracy × AI status cell is empty for all 69 home entries. The nearest work comes from other traditions. Sentience Institute's AIMS survey has polled US attitudes in waves (2021, 2023, 2024), but that measures uninformed opinion. Eleos, NYU CMEP and the Digital Sentience Consortium do expert and funding work. CoSI, which has democracy as a secondary tradition, maps arguments about functionalism but does not deliberate. Democracy X ran a citizens' panel on pig welfare that produced eight recommendations in April 2026, so the method carries over directly to another contested question about non-human moral status. Success would be published recommendations from a randomly selected panel on concrete questions (welfare assessments, letting models end conversations, labelling companion AIs), heard from both functionalists and sceptics, with AIMS items used before and after to measure how deliberation shifts views. The risks: the topic is speculative and panels are sensitive to how experts frame it; the results could be used to inflate or dismiss claims; and Mind AI Commission attribution can harm users, so the panel should also hear from the minds-protection side (AI Psychological Research Coalition). The value to safety is uncertain, which is why confidence is only medium.
steps: Approach Democracy X and Eleos together to scope a Danish pilot.
Apply to the Digital Sentience Consortium / Longview Digital Minds RFP for funding.
Co-design measurement with Sentience Institute so that AIMS questions serve as the pre- and post-deliberation baseline.
If the pilot works, repeat it in one non-Western country to test cultural variation.
gaps.evidence: Democracy × AI status is one of four empty problem cells for this tradition. AI moral status has only 46 entries map-wide. Democracy X's recent work includes an April 2026 citizens' panel on pig welfare. A web search found deliberative polls on AI in the public sector, on high-risk AI and on creative industries, but none on AI consciousness or welfare.

gaps.title: Chaplains' crisis knowledge turned into companion-AI test scenarios and protocols
gaps.summary: Chatbot-induced delusions often take a religious form, with users believing the AI channels God or the universe. Yet chaplains and spiritual-emergency clinicians, who handle spiritual crises professionally, are only now learning AI vocabulary and have no route into how models are designed or tested. A project turning chaplaincy practice into red-team scenarios, referral thresholds and evaluation items for companion AI would fill the gap.
gaps.detail: A web check found that the knowledge flows only one way. The Association of Professional Chaplains released an AI vocabulary for chaplains (June 2026), and the Chaplaincy Innovation Lab runs AI-literacy webinars and courses. Nothing carries chaplaincy's codified ethics of presence, boundaries and referral into model behaviour. RAND's analysis of 43 AI-psychosis cases found users who believed they were talking to a higher power. On the map, the psych tradition covers AI-associated delusions (the Human Line Project; KCL's Department of Psychosis Studies), but neither brings spiritual-care expertise. The AI Christian Benchmark's 'attachment' score (for example, models offering to pray) is the only religious test touching this. FBK-ISR's work on solitude and the Cambridge Interfaith Programme's 'one-person dialogue' argument supply the theory. Success would be an open set of a few hundred spiritual-crisis scenarios, with chaplain-written good responses and referral thresholds, adopted in at least one lab's or evaluation group's companion-safety tests. A second strand, linked to the conscience clause in the Oxford Oath for AI practitioners (OCTAI), could offer pastoral support to AI-lab staff, since the people-doing-the-work problem appears on only 2 of 50 entries. The risks: privacy of crisis material, the Christian and US skew of professional chaplaincy, and labs preferring clinical framings over spiritual ones.
steps: Pair the Chaplaincy Innovation Lab and the APC's ETHOS project with the Human Line Project or KCL's psychosis researchers to scope a shared protocol.
Collect anonymised patterns of spiritual-crisis conversations from chaplains and spiritual-emergency clinicians, under a published consent policy.
Write and release around 200 scenario items, test ten widely used models, and publish the results with referral guidance companies can adopt.
Pilot a small, confidential pastoral-support offer for AI-lab staff with OCTAI and multi-faith chaplains.
gaps.evidence: Protecting minds appears on 11 of 50 religion entries; people doing the work on 2; into the builders on 1 (OCTAI). Chaplaincy Lab is potential with no AI programme. Discovery gap: 'chatbot-induced spiritual and mystical delusions are a live 2025-26 harm… clear founder gap'. Gap (h): no faith body offers pastoral support to AI-lab staff.

gaps.title: Community-governed red-teaming in African and Indigenous languages for safety institutes
gaps.summary: Safeguards are weakest in low-resource languages. Masakhane, Te Hiku and Tattle hold the data, the communities and the skills to test them, but nothing on the map links them to the safety institutes' evaluation work, and no terms exist that keep red-team prompts under community control. A funded red-teaming and benchmark programme that respects data sovereignty would give this tradition its first solid foothold in assurance.
gaps.detail: Masakhane (over 1,000 participants, with a grant-making Hub funded by FCDO, IDRC and Gates) joined the Global South Network for Trustworthy AI in February 2026 and plans multilingual safety benchmarks. Tattle (a bridge entry that draws on this tradition) already builds multilingual evaluations. Te Hiku Media's Kaitiakitanga Licence is a template for keeping evaluation data out of training sets. Some multilingual testing already exists: Singapore's 2024-25 regional red-teaming challenge and the AI Safety Institute network's joint testing covered several Asian languages. I did not confirm in this pass which African or Indigenous languages they included. The opening is therefore the long tail of languages plus the governance terms, not multilingual testing as such. Success would be a benchmark in ten or more African and Indigenous languages, used in at least one safety-institute or lab pre-deployment evaluation, with contributors paid and the data licensed on community terms. Risks: communities doing unpaid safety work for labs; evaluation data leaking into training; capability gains for those languages that some communities may not want; and Te Hiku's technical output, which has slowed since 2023.
steps: Fund a safety red-teaming strand within the Masakhane African Languages Hub's next grant cycle, co-funded with IDRC AI4D and FCDO.
Draft a Kaitiakitanga-style licence for evaluation data with Te Hiku Media, so prompts and transcripts cannot be used for training.
Broker an agreement with UK AISI, or another institute in the network, to run the benchmark in pre-deployment testing, with CeRAI and Tattle as technical partners.
gaps.evidence: The Indigenous × Assurance cell holds one entry (Masakhane), the only assurance tag in the tradition. Tattle is a bridge with indigenous as a secondary tradition. Global South TAI Network is a bridge. No safety funder appears among Masakhane's funders. the discovery notes (b): nothing links planned multilingual benchmarks to the safety institutes' evaluation pipelines.

gaps.title: Wire Indigenous consent labels into AI training-data pipelines
gaps.summary: Tools for collective consent and provenance over data already exist, but nothing connects them to the tools that assemble and audit training corpora: Local Contexts' TK and BC Labels with their Hub API, GIDA's CARE Principles and IEEE 2890-2025, and Te Hiku's Kaitiakitanga Licence. A small technical and governance project could map them onto the preference signals and provenance tools dataset builders already use, then pilot the result on an open corpus.
gaps.detail: Local Contexts is coded no AI work yet: its site has no AI work. Its September 2026 guidance with Creative Commons pairs the Labels with CC licences, but my search found nothing linking them to CC signals or to tools for filtering training data. Creative Commons (which runs CC signals) and Data Provenance Init. are both on the map as adjacent and are natural technical partners. Provenance matters for safety as well as rights: knowing what a model absorbed, and on whose terms, is part of assurance and model documentation. Success would look like this: open-corpus builders and at least one lab honour the Labels, including a 'no AI use' state, when filtering; model documentation reports Indigenous data provenance; and AI Safety Institutes ask about it. Risks: the Labels could become consent-washing; communities may prefer outright refusal to machine-readable permissions; the signals cannot be enforced; Local Contexts and GIDA must lead and may decline; and x-risk funders may see the safety link as indirect, so Humanity AI or Mellon (which already funds Local Contexts) are likelier backers.
steps: Fund a scoping workshop led by Local Contexts and GIDA, with Creative Commons and the Data Provenance Initiative, to agree which Label and Notice states map to which machine-readable signals, refusal included.
Build an open-source annotator that reads Local Contexts Hub API and IEEE 2890 metadata and flags or excludes records, then test it on an open pretraining corpus.
Use Old Ways, New's reviewer seat on the International AI Safety Report and Te Mana Raraunga's submission practice to propose a data-provenance line in evaluation and model documentation.
gaps.evidence: Local Contexts is in the potential ring with transfer no AI work yet. GIDA, Te Hiku Media and Te Mana Raraunga are all coded 'standards'. 0 of 15 entries are on the classic map. The Indigenous × Assurance cell holds only one entry (Masakhane). the discovery notes (c): these governance tools 'appear on no AI-safety map'. One search found no integration of the Labels into AI pipelines.

gaps.title: Writers and narratologists on alignment pretraining data
gaps.summary: Geodesic Research has shown that how AI is described in training data shapes how models behave, and Hyperstition AI now generates whole novels about kind AI to shift that balance. Neither works with professional writers, narratologists or game designers, the people who know how stories form character. A pilot pairing them would test whether crafted narrative moves model behaviour more than generated text does.
gaps.detail: The arts tradition on the map is dominated by work on how publics and decision-makers picture AI (35 of its 46 entries tag sensemaking), and only two entries move narrative into the model. Narrative scholarship that could inform this sits nearby: the Center for Digital Narrative in Bergen (with its AI STORIES project), Arizona State's Center for Science and the Imagination, and Mark Riedl's lab at Georgia Tech, whose earlier work taught agents values from stories. Success would be a pre-registered comparison on an open-weight model of crafted, generated and baseline corpora against misalignment evaluations, with the corpus released under an open licence. Risks: effects may be small; such data could slide into public relations; writers' consent and pay must be explicit.
steps: Convene Geodesic Research and Hyperstition AI with Riedl's lab, the Center for Digital Narrative and ASU's Center for Science and the Imagination to agree a protocol.
Commission a few hundred short works under an open licence, with writers paid and credited, alongside generated and baseline controls.
Run the comparison on an open-weight model with standard misalignment and sycophancy evaluations, and publish null results as readily as positive ones.
gaps.evidence: Arts tradition: 46 entries, 35 tagged sensemaking, 2 that move knowledge into the model (Geodesic Research, Hyperstition AI). Arts, futures × People and arts x AI moral status are empty cells.

gaps.title: Fellowship bringing treaty-verification inspectors into AI-agreement verification work
gaps.summary: Proposals for international AI agreements depend on verification, yet the people who have actually run inspection regimes (IAEA, CTBTO, OPCW, VERTIC) are not on the map. A placement fellowship modelled on IST's AI–Nuclear Policy Accelerator, plus bridge funding for the one interdisciplinary verification group already on the map, would move that practical knowledge across.
gaps.detail: Arms-control verification has decades of practical experience that AI-agreement design needs: declarations, managed access, challenge inspections, and building technical bodies that rival states both trust. On the map, the verification work sits with researchers. PRIF EDT / CNTR (CNTR) combines physicists, computer scientists and political scientists, but its funding period ends in December 2026 with no renewal confirmed. IFSH Arms Control & ET has a 2026 paper on AI assurance for the OPCW, and Oxford Martin AIGI has published on verification for international AI governance. IST's accelerator, funded by Andrew Carnegie Fdn, already gave 26 nuclear practitioners AI literacy, which shows the placement model works. Success would be a cohort of 10-15 former inspectors and verification scientists placed in AI governance organisations and national AI safety institutes, producing joint designs for compute and model-verification regimes. Risks: technical work on compute verification already exists inside AI governance, so the fellowship should bring regime-design and inspection know-how rather than duplicate hardware research. Former inspectors may also be bound by confidentiality.
steps: Approach CNTR before December 2026 about bridge funding that keeps its verification group alive while a fellowship is designed.
Recruit a first cohort through VERTIC, CTBTO and OPCW alumni networks and the PRIF and IFSH arms-control networks, and place fellows with Oxford Martin AIGI, IST or national AI safety institutes.

Ask each fellow for a short design paper on one verifiable AI commitment (for example a compute threshold or a model-evaluation obligation), tested in a tabletop exercise with Stanford CISAC or UNIDIR.
gaps.evidence: No verification body (IAEA, CTBTO, OPCW, VERTIC) is on the map, and gap (b) in the discovery notes says this expertise has barely reached compute governance. PRIF EDT / CNTR's funding ends in December 2026. IST's accelerator (26 fellows) is the model to copy. A quick search found academic papers on lessons from nuclear verification for AI treaties and a CTBTO fellowship limited to nuclear work, but no AI verification placement scheme.

gaps.title: Model safety clauses for collective agreements at labs and data suppliers
gaps.summary: The map has 17 labour organisations: 16 are framed around present harms, and the only bridge is the UTAW/Unite campaign at Google DeepMind. No AI-safety organisation works with unions. A small unit that drafts and tests safety clauses would give the field a lever with legal force: safety representatives, a right to refuse unsafe deployment, whistleblower protection, and fair-work standards for the people who do RLHF and red-teaming.
gaps.detail: UTAW members asked Google for recognition in May 2026. Google refused but agreed to ACAS talks limited to pay, holidays and hours, so what can be bargained over is now the live question. The material for a clause bank already exists: the TUC's model AI bill (drafted by Robin Allen KC and Dee Masters), UK health-and-safety representative law, IFOW's impact assessments, Fairwork's AI principles and supplier audits (Sama, Appen), and the data-worker code of conduct from Aapti Institute and Karya. On the supply side, Alphabet Workers Union has organised Google's AI raters, and Data Labelers (DLA) (878+ members, Nairobi) and Data Workers' Inquiry speak for the people who produce safety-relevant labels. Success would be a clause bank used in at least one recognition agreement, and a safety funder or lab committing to Fairwork standards for its red-teaming and RLHF suppliers. The risks: labs will resist, the work may be seen as partisan, unions may put job losses ahead of safety, and lab funding could co-opt worker voice.
steps: Fund the TUC model-bill drafters or IFOW to draft a short clause bank on safety representatives, the right to refuse, and whistleblower protection, adapted from UK health-and-safety law.
Offer it to UTAW/Unite and AWU-CWA for their campaigns, with AIWI advising on protections.
Ask safety funders and labs to adopt Fairwork's AI principles for their RLHF and red-teaming suppliers, with Data Labelers (DLA) and Data Workers' Inquiry consulted on the terms.
int/a's London hub convenes UTAW, the TUC, IFOW and AIWI; all four are in London.
gaps.evidence: organised labour: 17 entries, 16 adjacent, 1 bridge, 0 core, and all 17 framed as present harms or structural and gradual. The membership-bodies notes found no union framing AI as a civilisation-scale loss of bargaining power, and no AI-safety organisation working with unions. 8 economics entries tag 'people'.

gaps.title: Human-rights due diligence for frontier AI, tested through investors
gaps.summary: In September 2026 the UN human rights chief asked frontier AI companies for human-rights due diligence that includes agreed safety standards, incident reporting and independent monitoring. Nobody has yet written what that means for catastrophic or existential risks. A joint team from business-and-human-rights and frontier-safety evaluation would write that protocol and pilot it, using investors and national human rights institutions to press for adoption.
gaps.detail: The UN Guiding Principles already rank harms by scale, scope and irremediability, a test that fits catastrophic or existential, irreversible risks better than most AI-ethics frameworks. They come with tools already in use: OHCHR B-Tech's foundation-model papers and its product workstream with BSR (adjacent), DIHR's guide to fundamental rights impact assessments and its NHRI Digital Rights Alliance (adjacent), the Council of Europe's HUDERIA method (adjacent), OECD National Contact Points, and engagement by faith-based investors through ICCR and the Investor Alliance for Human Rights (religion>law, adjacent). Frontier safety frameworks set capability thresholds and evaluations, but they offer no rights-based remedy and no external route for complaints. None of the 93 law entries connects the two sides. Success would be a published protocol that maps the elements of frontier safety frameworks onto the Guiding Principles' steps. It would be used in at least one investor engagement and one NHRI review, and cited by AISIs. There are three risks. Due diligence can turn into box-ticking. Rights groups such as Derechos Digitales and Fundación Vía Libre are sceptical of x-risk framing. And labs may welcome a soft standard as a way to avoid regulation, so the protocol has to keep the Guiding Principles' remedy and independent-monitoring elements.
steps: Bring B-Tech, DIHR and a frontier evaluator (an AISI or an independent evaluation group) together for a short drafting sprint on how the Guiding Principles' test of severity maps onto capability thresholds and incident reporting.
Pilot it with ICCR members and other responsible investors that hold shares in frontier-lab parent companies, as engagement asks for the 2027 AGM season.
Ask one national human rights institution, DIHR, to review a lab's published safety framework against the protocol.
Feed the results into the Council of Europe Convention's Conference of the Parties and the UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance.
gaps.evidence: Türk's letter of September 2026 asks frontier AI companies for exactly this. B-Tech, DIHR, the Council of Europe and ICCR are all adjacent, and all transfer into institutions. Of 93 law profiles, 52 are framed around present harms and 2 around catastrophic or existential risk. The sociotech discovery notes list this as a bridge no organisation owns.

gaps.title: A desk turning chatbot-harm court records into evidence on lab safety
gaps.summary: Chatbot-harm lawsuits produce filings, expert reports and testimony about how labs tested and shipped their models. Nobody reads these as safety evidence, and settlements can bury them. A small legal-research desk would collect, code and publish what the public record shows, and push for settlements and remedies that disclose more.
gaps.detail: The Tech Justice Law Project (bridge) was counsel in Garcia v. Character Technologies, and in 2026 it filed Carrier and Lines v. OpenAI Foundation. In January 2026 Character.AI and Google agreed to settle five teen-harm suits, Garcia among them, which shows how quickly evidence can vanish into settlements. Trackers exist, such as TJLP's TRAL tracker with Knight-Georgetown and Georgetown CCT, but they count cases. They do not extract what the cases reveal about evaluations, red-teaming, known risks and decisions to ship. Others need that factual base: the ALI's Principles of the Law on civil liability for AI (adjacent), OII's 'careless speech' work, and safety researchers writing about lab practice. Success would be a public, coded record of the safety-relevant facts in every major AI-harm case, cited by AISIs, the ALI reporters and model-spec authors. It would also mean settlement terms that require disclosure and independent monitoring. The risks are real. Protective orders and sealed discovery limit what is public. The desk could look like plaintiff advocacy, so it needs a neutral host such as a law-school clinic, with input from defence lawyers. And most cases concern companion harms rather than catastrophic or existential risk, although what they show about how labs decide to ship carries over.
steps: List the AI-harm dockets (the OpenAI and Character.AI suicide and psychosis suits, Social Media Victims Law Center cases, the FTC's 2025 orders to companion-chatbot makers) and code public filings against a template drawn from frontier safety frameworks.
Host the desk in a US law-school clinic, with advisers from TJLP and the defence bar and one safety researcher to frame the coding.
Where protective orders cover safety-relevant material, file public-interest motions to unseal, and draft model settlement terms with disclosure and independent-monitor clauses.
Publish a brief twice a year for AISIs, the ALI reporters and lab safety teams.
gaps.evidence: Law, society × Assurance has 34 entries, but only 4 of 93 law entries transfer into the model. TJLP is the only litigation organisation on the map. The sociotech discovery notes list this as an unowned bridge ('litigation-to-safety translation desk'). Garcia was settled in January 2026.

gaps.title: An African philosophy research line inside Africa's AI-safety organisations
gaps.summary: Africa's AI-safety organisations work in law, policy and technical fields, and none draws on philosophy. The one African philosophy entry on the map has been inactive since 2022. A funded philosophy line, hosted by an existing safety body, would bring Ubuntu and other African relational ethics into alignment targets and debates on moral status.
gaps.detail: Ubuntu-based AI ethics is now a substantial academic literature: Sabelo Mhlambi's work, a 2026 dissertation on Ubuntu as a paradigm for AI governance, and proposals to build it into African health-AI research ethics. Emma Ruttkamp-Bloem of the University of Pretoria chaired the expert group that drafted UNESCO's 2021 Recommendation, and she co-authored a 2026 Delphi study ranking AI risks. Yet the discovery notes found Ubuntu scholars and no organisation, and her CAIR group (CAIR Ethics of AI (UP)) shows no activity after 2022. Meanwhile Africa's safety bodies are growing: ILINA (core, on the classic map), African AI Safety Hub (launched by UCT and GCG), CISAI and Equiano Institute. Success would be a 2-3 year research line with a few fellows, hosted by one of these bodies. It would publish on, for example, what relational personhood implies for AI moral status (a direct input to Eleos AI and NYU CMEP) and what communal consent implies for public input to model specs, and it would feed the multi-tradition spec review above. The risks are presenting Ubuntu as one doctrine, thin senior capacity, and drifting back into general AI ethics without a safety question.
steps: Approach African AI Safety Hub and GCG about hosting one or two philosophy fellows.
Ask Emma Ruttkamp-Bloem whether the Pretoria CAIR ethics group could be revived around AI risk and moral status.
Fund 3-5 African philosophy fellowships attached to ILINA's existing fellowship.
Commission one paper on Ubuntu personhood and AI moral status, and put it into the digital-minds field's venues.
gaps.evidence: Philosophy by region: Sub-Saharan Africa 1 (CAIR Ethics of AI (UP), unverified, last activity 2022), Latin America & Caribbean 0, Middle East, North Africa 0. Of the 11 African organisations on the whole map, none lists philosophy as a tradition. Angle notes (faith/knowledge traditions, gap d): 'Ubuntu has scholars ... but no organisation'. A web search (Oct 2026) found academic Ubuntu-AI work but no standing centre.

economics.overview: Economics brings five things to making AI go well: the political economy of power concentration and lock-in, the economics of transformative AI (windfalls, public finance, labour markets), institutional designs for commons, cooperatives and public AI, organised labour, and the macroprudential toolkit that financial supervisors use to watch whole systems of correlated agents. The map has 56 organisations with economics as their home tradition (6 core, 8 bridge, 40 adjacent, 2 potential), and another 62 draw on it as a secondary tradition, including core groups such as Forethought, ACS Research, MAI, AOI and FLF. The main actors are unions (17 labour entries), commons and public-AI groups (17), financial-stability bodies (5 of the 8 bridge entries) and a small x-risk cluster on power concentration (Formation Research, Longview Power RFP, Post-AGI Workshop). The tradition sits well away from the core: 40 of the 56 are adjacent, 35 work by pushing ideas into institutions, only 2 use a catastrophic or existential framing (Convergence Analysis, KIRA Center), and just 3 are on the aisafety.com map.
economics.missing: Nothing on the map carries economics into the AI systems themselves or into the agent economies now being built. The Economics × Agency, values and AI moral status cells are empty, only 2 of 56 entries tag multi-agent AI, and the map has no competition authority, industrial-organisation (IO) economist or market-design group, even though LLM pricing agents already collude in experiments and companies are building agent payment rails.

religion.overview: Religion brings three things the AI-safety field lacks: a constituency of billions, norm-setting machinery that already issues AI rulings (the Holy See's Magnifica Humanitas, Resolution 258 of the International Islamic Fiqh Academy (IIFA), the Riyadh Charter of the Islamic world's education and culture agency ICESCO, responsa from the Central Conference of American Rabbis (CCAR), the Southern Baptist ethics agency's statement), and long traditions of thought about dignity, conscience and formation. The main actors are the Holy See, the World Council of Churches (WCC), the IIFA and ICESCO, AI and Faith, Notre Dame's DELTA, the faith-university benchmark consortium CEFEAI, 84000 with the Buddhism & AI Initiative, and two funders: FLI (Future of Life Institute) and Templeton (JTF). The tradition sits far from the core: of its 50 organisations, 1 is core, 9 are bridge, 26 adjacent and 14 potential. Only 1 is on the aisafety.com map, and just 1 frames the stakes as catastrophic or existential. 45 of the 50 work on meaning and dignity, and 36 only convene their own community.
religion.missing: Nobody acts as a standing translator between religious norm-setters and frontier risk. The bodies whose rulings reach billions (IIFA, ICESCO, CCAR, the Southern Baptist ethics agency, the Holy See) cover permissibility, dignity and disclosure, but none addresses loss of control. The field's main bridge into these bodies is a round of one-year FLI grants. The map is also US- and Abrahamic-heavy: 20 of 50 entries are in North America, and there is no Hindu, Sikh, Jain, Shinto, Daoist, Bahá'í, Pentecostal or African-instituted body. That gap is partly a search artefact.

minds.overview: Consciousness and AI minds brings philosophy of Mind AI Commission, consciousness science and animal-sentience methods to the question of whether AI systems could be subjects with welfare, and what that means for how they are built, tested, retired and governed. Its 28 home organisations sit unusually close to the core: 11 core and 11 bridge. Ten of the 11 core entries were founded in 2024–26: Eleos AI, PRISM, Cambridge Digital Minds, RP AI Cognition' Digital Consciousness Model, Anthropic Model Welfare, Digital Sentience Consortium, Reciprocal Research, Anima Labs and others. The core is a tight network funded by EA sources (Navigation Fund, Macroscopic/Polaris, Longview, SFF, Coefficient Giving) and based in English-speaking countries: 19 of 28 are in North America or the UK and Ireland, and none in Africa, Latin America or MENA. Mainstream consciousness science (Sussex, AMCS, Arizona, Copenhagen CFS, NIAS) sits at the edge and is often sceptical. Fifteen more organisations elsewhere on the map draw on this tradition, mostly NeuroAI (AE Studio Alignment, Astera Institute, levin-lab), contemplative science (Monash M3CS, flourishing and positive-intelligence-program) and AI-rights advocacy (UFAIR, The Signal Front).
minds.missing: No one on the map comes from the clinical sciences that judge consciousness in beings who cannot report it reliably: disorders-of-consciousness medicine, anaesthesiology (the only anaesthetist on the map is Hameroff, there for quantum theory) and practical animal-welfare assessment. These are the closest existing practices to 'welfare assessment under uncertainty about self-report', yet the field is building its AI indicators mainly from philosophy.

philosophy.overview: Philosophy gives the AI transition its accounts of value, agency, moral status and legitimacy, and through applied ethics it gives institutions for governing contested technologies. The map has 52 organisations with philosophy as their home tradition: 10 core, 10 bridge, 31 adjacent and 1 potential, with 7 on the aisafety.com map. Another 70 draw on philosophy as a secondary tradition, mostly in the AI-minds, religion and contemplative clusters. For a humanities tradition it sits close to the core (38% core or bridge), but that closeness belongs to one school. All 14 moral-philosophy entries are core or bridge (Forethought, CRS, Macroscopic Ventures, MINT Lab, MAI and others), and most are funded by EA or SFF money. The ethics councils, bioethics institutes and continental or Asian philosophy-of-technology groups sit almost entirely in the adjacent ring, with no safety framing.
philosophy.missing: Nothing on the map carries applied ethics' governance machinery into frontier-AI decisions: research-ethics review, independent monitoring boards with stopping rules, and standing pluralist ethics councils. Nor does anything bring non-EA moral traditions to bear on the value documents labs now publish. The safety field has adopted one school's theories of value and almost none of philosophy's institutions or its non-Western traditions.

life.overview: Life & systems sciences bring the study of self-organising wholes to AI safety: how parts become agents, how they cooperate or defect (cancer, collusion), how systems regulate themselves, and how they collapse. The map holds 49 organisations here (10 core, 13 bridge, 8 adjacent, 18 potential; 7 on the aisafety.com map). A further 57 draw on life as a secondary tradition. The main actors are Principles of Intelligence (the talent pipeline), ACS Research, Softmax, XOR Labs, Equilibria Network, Astera and AE Studio, funded mostly by SFF and Jed McCaleb. Templeton is the largest money in diverse intelligence but has no safety track. The tradition sits closer to the core than most (20% core against 14% across the map), but only through its agent-science half. Its cybernetics, ecology and systems half sits far out.
life.missing: Nothing translates the systems half of the tradition into AI-safety research. Its 16 cybernetics, systems and ecology entries have no core organisation and none on the classic map, 9 are potential, and most only convene. Across all 49 entries the tradition also contributes nothing to Protecting its constituency minds or meaning, and has only one entry whose primary problem is assurance.

indigenous.overview: This tradition gives the safety field two things it lacks. The first is working tools for collective consent, provenance and community authority over data and models: the CARE Principles, IEEE 2890-2025, the TK and BC Labels and the Kaitiakitanga Licence. The second is a set of relational ontologies that approach AI through kinship, reciprocity and obligation instead of control. Its 15 home organisations fall into two groups. Indigenous-led knowledge and data-sovereignty bodies: Abundant Intelligences, Te Hiku Media, GIDA, Te Mana Raraunga, Local Contexts and Old Ways, New. Decolonial, Black and feminist groups: DAIR, Masakhane, Coding Rights, A+ Alliance and Technecultura. Six other organisations draw on the tradition as a secondary one (Tattle, IT for Change, lavits, Bioneers, SAND, Histories of AI (Camb.)). It sits further from the AI-safety core than any other tradition on the map. It has no core entries and one bridge (Old Ways, New, through its founder's reviewer seat on the International AI Safety Report). None of its organisations is on the aisafety.com map. Its funders (IDRC, FCDO, MacArthur, Mellon, Kellogg, the 11th Hour Project) are entirely separate from safety money, and some members, DAIR above all, openly oppose the x-risk framing.
indigenous.missing: Nobody translates between this tradition and the safety core with Indigenous consent. As a result, its relational ontology never reaches the problems about the AI itself, and its working consent tools never reach training-data or evaluation pipelines. That is why 0 of 15 are on the classic map and no x-risk funder backs any of them. The discovery pass for this tradition also ran with no web searches, so the potential and bridge rings are under-sampled.

democracy.overview: Democracy and collective intelligence brings two things to making AI go well. The first is the machinery of legitimacy for deciding together about AI: sortition, deliberative polling, consensus conferences and broad listening. The second is collective-epistemics tools: forecasting, argument mapping, fact-checking and provenance. The tradition has 68 home entries (12 core, plus Coefficient Giving counted as a generalist funder; 14 bridge, 37 adjacent, 5 potential), and 51 more organisations use it as a secondary tradition, most of them in law (Ada Lovelace, the Knight Institute, Weizenbaum) or elsewhere (MAI, Metagov, Toda). The main actors are CIP, the AI & Democracy Foundation, AOI and Odyssean at the core; Stanford DDL, DemocracyNext, CompDem/Polis and g0v/vTaiwan as bridges; a forecasting cluster (FRI, Metaculus, Sage, AI Impacts, Sentinel); and a dense band of adjacent civic-tech toolmakers (Harmonica, Dembrane, deliberAIde, Jigsaw, Make.org, DD2030/Team Mirai). Ten entries are on the aisafety.com map, the most of any Society & institutions tradition. Even so, only the forecasting half sits near the safety core; the deliberative half stays mostly adjacent.
democracy.missing: The tradition's legitimacy methods have not reached the decisions the safety field cares about most. Only 6 of 69 entries use a catastrophic or existential framing (5 of them forecasters), and only 2 deliberation organisations are core (Odyssean, whose assembly is still a proposal, and AIDF). No institution puts frontier-AI thresholds, pauses or AI moral status to representative publics, and nobody independently audits the AI mediators that now run public deliberations.

psych.overview: Psychology and cognitive science bring three things to AI going well. First, evidence on what AI does to human minds: clinical, developmental and relationship research. Second, methods for studying models as behavioural subjects: machine psychology, cognitive science and wisdom measurement. Third, care for the people doing AI-safety work. The map holds 65 organisations with psych as their home tradition (6 core, 15 bridge, 38 adjacent, 6 potential; 5 on the aisafety.com map) and 68 more that draw on it as a secondary tradition. The main actors form a clinical cluster (KCL Psychosis Studies, the Aarhus group, BIDMC Digital Psychiatry, Stanford Brainstorm, the Human Line Project, AIPRC), a youth cluster (Common Sense Media's Youth AI Safety Institute, everyone.AI, Fairplay, Young Futures), a few machine-psychology groups (Hagendorff's team at IRIS Stuttgart, Helmholtz HCA, Re-Align), Grossmann's Wisdom and Culture Lab, and UK AISI's Human Influence team. The tradition sits far from the core in its own right. Of the 65, 47 address Protecting its constituency minds, 29 work by Protecting its constituency their own constituency, and only 5 use a catastrophic or existential framing. Psychology mostly reaches the core as a secondary ingredient of organisations homed elsewhere.
psych.missing: No organisation on the map studies the psychology of the people and institutions steering AI: safety culture in labs, groupthink, escalation and how decision-makers perceive the race. Psychology × Security and Psychology × Metacrisis are empty, and power has one entry (CHT). The taxonomy has no organisational or political psychology sub-tradition. Psychology on the map studies users, children and patients and looks after safety workers, but never examines the collective minds of the decision-makers. It also has no Majority-World organisation at all: 0 of 65.

safety.overview: Safety and risk sciences bring the practical know-how that made aviation, nuclear power, medicine and finance safer: system-safety engineering and safety cases (York CfAA, MIT PSASS, CSR City St George's, SCSC, SAE G-34 / WG-114, ULSE (UL 4600)), measurement science (NPL AI Measurement, PTB AI-Met), incident learning (AIID, AIAAIC, OECD AIM, ECRI), risk management and insurance (SaferAI, CLTR, AIUC, five actuarial bodies), and public health and biosecurity (JHU Health Security, SecureBio). The AI-safety field borrows more visibly from this tradition than from any other, yet most of it sits outside the field. Of 66 placed organisations, 9 are core, 27 bridge, 23 adjacent and 7 potential, and only 3 are on the aisafety.com map (CLTR, SaferAI, CARMA). Most of the bridges deal with narrow deployed autonomy such as cars, aircraft and clinical tools, not general-purpose systems, and 48 of 67 frame AI as a present harm. Biosecurity is the one strand that has fully crossed over: SecureBio runs pre-release evaluations of frontier models.
safety.missing: The cultural and institutional half of safety science is missing. That means safety culture, just culture, high-reliability organising, confidential near-miss reporting, independent accident investigation and industry peer review on the INPO/WANO model. The tradition has no entries in the We quadrant, and only one of its entries (the CAIS course) aims at the people who build AI. Nobody yet applies these institutions to frontier developers.

contemplative.overview: Contemplative and integral traditions bring first-person, practice-based knowledge of Mind AI Commission: what selfhood, attachment, attention and care are, and how they can be trained. They also bring a science of meditators, and the integral and metamodern milieu int/a itself comes from. The map holds 40 organisations with this home tradition (2 core, 11 bridge, 4 adjacent, 23 potential), plus 7 that draw on it secondarily, among them 84000, the Buddhism & AI Initiative and QRI. The part facing AI safety is about a dozen small, mostly new bodies: a science cluster turning Buddhist ideas into alignment targets (CSAS, FLIP, M3CS, Mathematical Metaphysics Institute, Groundless Alignment, Positive AI Labs) and a practice cluster forming AI builders (MAPLE, Wisdom + AI, Wisdom Beyond, Wisdom 2.0). It sits far from the core: none of the 40 is on the aisafety.com map, 33 frame the stakes as flourishing and positive and only MAPLE as catastrophic or existential, and half (20) belong to the integral and metamodern milieu, which gathers its own audience but has almost no AI-safety literacy.
contemplative.missing: No contemplative claim about AI has yet been tested against the safety field's own evaluations. The seven groups that aim to change models rest on essays, prompting experiments and documents given to one lab, and the one group set up to build evaluations (Positive AI Labs) has published none. Behind this is money: the contemplative world's own funders make no AI grants, so its large institutions only convene, while its AI work depends on a few SFF and Templeton grants.

formal.overview: The formal tradition brings mathematics, theoretical physics, theoretical computer science, logic, statistics, and decision and game theory to AI safety. It uses them to define, explain and verify what AI systems are and do. The main actors are a dense cluster around Principles of Intelligence and Iliad (AIXI Labs, Stormglass, Alignment Journal, AFFINE, Dovetail); well-funded theory labs (Resolution, MAISI, Simplex, CORAL); ARIA's category-theory programme (ARIA Safeguarded AI, Topos Institute, GLAIVE); cooperative game theory (FOCAL (CMU), Modeling Cooperation, the Teesside group, the PIK group at Potsdam); and an outer ring of statistics, metrology and decision-science societies. It sits closer to the AI-safety core than any other tradition: half of its 30 organisations are core and a third are on aisafety.com's map, against 14% and 9% across the whole map.
formal.missing: The missing formal disciplines are the ones aimed at how people decide rather than at the model itself: social choice, decision analysis under deep uncertainty, and measurement science. They sit in the potential ring or are absent from the map. No formal-rooted organisation works on democratic voice, meaning, or the moral status of AI.

law.overview: Law brings the tools societies already use to hold powerful actors to account: liability and litigation, human-rights law and due diligence, children's-rights design codes, treaties and whistleblower protection. Through STS and sociology it also brings field methods for studying how technologies are built and used. It is the largest tradition on the map (91 placed organisations, or 93 profiles counting the generalist funders CIFAR and Humanity AI). Its main actors include the Tech Justice Law Project, Hadfield's Normativity Lab, OHCHR B-Tech, the Council of Europe, CAIDP, 5Rights, Data & Society, the Ada Lovelace Institute, the Oxford Internet Institute and Schwartz Reisman, with Humanity AI, the European AI & Society Fund and IDRC's AI4D as funders. It sits far from the safety core: 62 adjacent, 19 bridge, 8 potential and only 2 core (AIWI and ILINA), with 3 on the aisafety.com map (AIWI, ILINA, PAI). Justice is the primary problem for 43 of 93, but bridges are forming through Global South safety work (GCG, Digital Futures Lab, the Global South Network) and through the UN rights chief's September 2026 letter warning frontier AI companies of existential risks.
law.missing: No legal organisation yet carries the rights-law tools (due diligence, litigation and remedies, treaty monitoring, statutory regulators) into frontier-safety practice. Nothing links the x-risk legal groups on the classic map (LawAI, CLAIR, LASST, Legal Safety Lab) with the 62 adjacent rights organisations. The gap is widest in Latin America: all 10 Latin American organisations on the whole map are adjacent, 8 of them rooted in law, and the regional safety groups that grew out of EA (LANAIS, BAISH, the LATAM fellowship) do not appear to work with them.

peace.overview: The peace tradition brings the oldest tested toolkit for handling dangerous technology between rivals: arms control and verification, confidence-building measures and hotlines, Track II and scientist-to-scientist diplomacy, the humanitarian-law doctrine of meaningful human control, and mediation. Its main actors fall into three clusters. The first is Track II channels: Safe AI Forum (SAIF), Concordia AI, Oxford Martin AIGI, Brookings-Tsinghua AI Dialogue and HD AI & Emerging Tech. The second is arms-control institutes, mostly funded by Andrew Carnegie Fdn: SIPRI, ELN Nuclear & Tech, IST, Pugwash and NTI. The third is humanitarian-law and UN bodies: ICRC autonomous weapons, Stop Killer Robots and UNIDIR. Peace sits fairly close to the AI-safety core: 28 of its 51 entries are core or bridge, and 6 are on the aisafety.com map. That closeness is almost entirely in diplomacy and arms control, and it reaches AI mostly through AI in nuclear command and military AI rather than frontier loss of control. Peacebuilding and mediation (11 entries) stay at adjacent and potential.
peace.missing: Peacebuilding's own knowledge is not being applied to AI itself: conflict analysis, mediation, ripeness, de-escalation and dialogue across enemies. Of the 11 peacebuilding entries, none is core and only HD AI & Emerging Tech is bridge. No peace organisation works on the race between labs or between the AI camps, or on conflict between AI agents. None of the 51 moves its knowledge into the model or to the builders.

arts.overview: Arts, narrative and futures brings imagination as a working method: the scenarios, wargames and stories through which publics and decision-makers picture AI, and the futures and technology-assessment bodies that turn foresight into policy. The map holds 46 organisations here (9 core, 11 bridge, 20 adjacent, 7 potential; 5 on the aisafety.com map). The core is scenario and narrative work inside the safety community, such as the AI Futures Project, Intelligence Rising, Existential Hope, Tarbell and Geodesic Research. The outer rings hold futures institutes (Copenhagen Institute for Futures Studies, Institute for the Future, Sitra, Europe's parliamentary technology-assessment offices), arts institutions (Serpentine Arts Technologies, AIxDESIGN, Better Images of AI) and the translators' and linguists' professional bodies.
arts.missing: Narrative Stanford CRAFT has barely met the finding that stories in training data shape model behaviour, and the futures profession itself (the World Futures Studies Federation, UNESCO Futures Literacy, the School of International Futures) has no sustained AI-risk programme, so the field's scenarios come almost entirely from forecasters inside it.

cellNotes.economics|potential: Two entries (Ostrom Workshop, OpenResearch). This is mostly an artefact of the search, with a real opening inside it. Economics engages with AI so heavily that many relevant bodies already run an AI programme and land in adjacent. But the discovery notes name pools that nobody swept: IO economists and competition authorities (none on the map), market and mechanism-design labs, development economists and resource-governance bodies, sovereign wealth funds, and cash-transfer researchers such as GiveDirectly (named only as OpenResearch's partner). The investor-stewardship sweep (CFA Institute, NBIM, PRI) stopped when the search budget ran out. A targeted pass would probably add 10-20 entries. The real opening is that these pools hold working methods and have had no contact with AI safety.
cellNotes.economics|core: Six entries, all political economy (Formation Research, Longview Power RFP, Post-AGI Workshop) or TAI economics (Windfall Trust, Convergence Analysis, KIRA Center). Commons and cooperatives have no core entry, and nor does organised labour. That gap is real: no cooperative, commons or labour body treats AI going well as its mission. A cheap move for int/a on the commons side: the two 'cooperative AI' communities, Platform Co-op Consortium (democratic ownership) and the game-theoretic one (FOCAL (CMU), CAIF), have had almost no contact, and one Convening its community could bring them together.
cellNotes.economics|bridge: Eight entries, but five of them are financial-stability bodies (FSB, BIS / FSI, Bank of England, ESRB, LSE Systemic Risk Centre). Each of the other sub-traditions has exactly one: commons (Funding the Commons), labour (UTAW (DeepMind union)) and power (Equiano Institute). The thin labour and commons cells are real: organised labour reaches AI safety through a single union branch's campaign at one lab. Several adjacent organisations are one framing away from bridge, notably IFOW, MIT Stone Center and Open Markets Institute, whose idea of 'AI lock-in' is close to Formation Research's.
cellNotes.religion|core: One entry: Project Imago Dei. It is a small evangelical initiative with a thin website and a $47,500 FLI grant. Mostly a real opening, partly a search artefact. Real, because no faith-rooted organisation whose primary mission is making AI go well was found. Christians for Impact is the nearest, but AI is one cause area among seven, so it is bridge. Artefact, because FLI's 2026 religious grantees were not profiled as separate organisations: the Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of America, Wheaton College, IBA Karachi, MENA Islamic scholars, the Hindu project through Impact Academy/SteadRise, and ILINA's African Faith & AI Initiative (ILINA itself is homed in law). Faith Matters Foundation's 'Organized Intelligence', noted in discovery, is also absent. If any of these becomes a standing organisation it would land here. A re-sweep of FLI's grantee list would settle how much of the gap is artefact.
cellNotes.religion|bridge: Nine entries, so not thin overall, but the sub-cells are. There is 1 Islamic/Jewish entry (Sinai and Synapses), and no Hindu or African entry at all. Five of the ten core and bridge entries owe their safety framing mainly to FLI grants. Those are fragile seeds that could slip back to adjacent once one-year funding ends, which shows how shallow this ring is.
cellNotes.religion|potential: Fourteen entries, all interfaith, Buddhist or Islamic/Jewish. Hindu, Sikh, Jain, Shinto, Daoist and Bahá'í bodies all came back 'searched, none found' or 'thin', but that sweep ran after the WebSearch budget was spent. It relied on fetching sites directly, and four key sites sat behind bot checks (KAICIID, the Bahá'í International Community, the Southern Baptist ethics agency, The Gospel Coalition). Treat this cell as a search artefact rather than evidence of absence. Pentecostal and African-instituted churches were never searched.
cellNotes.minds|adjacent: Only two entries: LSE Animal Sentience (AI's effects on animals) and Arizona CCS / TSC (a conference that treats AI consciousness as a topic). This is mostly a taxonomy artefact. Anyone who works on AI and minds without an x-risk or welfare frame is routed elsewhere: clinical work on Mind AI Commission attribution goes to psych, ethics to philosophy. And almost every new group on AI consciousness frames itself around welfare, which places it in bridge. One part is a real gap: work on how AI in farming, aquaculture and slaughter monitoring affects animal welfare (veterinary and welfare-science bodies) appears only through Coller. A non-English search could also find Japanese and Chinese consciousness groups that discuss AI without any welfare framing.
cellNotes.minds|potential: Four entries (QRI, Essentia Foundation, CFS Copenhagen, NIAS Consciousness Studies). That is above the threshold but thin, given how large consciousness science is. Much of this is a search artefact. The neuro sweep's search budget ran out, and it dropped the Wisconsin Center for Sleep and Consciousness, Graziano's lab, the Kempner Institute and Mind & Life because it could not verify an AI link. ASSC, Kavli, Simons and Allen hold relevant knowledge but have no AI programme. One part is a real gap: the map has no disorders-of-consciousness or anaesthesia research group at all (for example Liège's Coma Science Group, or the labs behind command-following imaging and perturbational complexity measures), although their methods address the AI-welfare problem directly.
cellNotes.philosophy|potential: One entry (Center for Process Studies). This is mostly an artefact of classification and search, not a sign that philosophy lacks latent partners. 18 potential-ring organisations draw on philosophy as a secondary tradition but are homed elsewhere: 7 in contemplative (Perspectiva, Metamoderna, The Stoa, Nordic Bildung and others), plus UChicago Wisdom Center, CFS Copenhagen, Essentia Foundation and NIAS Consciousness Studies. The philosophy sweep ran out of web searches after 14 queries and left candidates unverified: HKU's AI & Humanity Lab, Duke's Moral AI project, Institut Jean Nicod (site failed certificate checks), the Kyoto Institute of Philosophy and IZEW Tübingen. There is a structural and gradual reason too: academic philosophers engage with AI as individuals, so a department with light AI engagement rarely shows up as a unit. A targeted sweep would probably add 10-20 entries. The likely real gaps are philosophy-of-science and measurement groups (on construct validity of evals), military-ethics and just-war centres, pragmatist traditions, and Latin American and Indian academic philosophy. All four are hypotheses until searched.
cellNotes.philosophy|bridge: Ten entries, so not thin overall. One sub-cell is empty, though: applied ethics and councils have 0 bridge entries out of 18 (17 adjacent, 1 core). This looks like a real gap, not an artefact. The councils were searched and verified (German Ethics Council, CCNEN, EGE, Nuffield Bioethics, Hastings Center), and each has a live AI line framed only around present harms or rights. Hastings's one safety-style project, funded by FLI with Stuart Russell, ended in 2019. Separately, VALAWAI ended on 30 September 2026 with no follow-on project, so the bridge cell is about to lose its only EU-funded value-aware AI project.
cellNotes.philosophy|core: Ten entries, not thin, but lopsided: 8 are moral philosophy, mostly longtermist or suffering-focused. There is one philosophy-of-technology entry (Beijing-AISI, state-backed) and one applied-ethics entry (Creed Space, which is a software tool, not an ethics body). This looks like a real pattern: the safety ecosystem's funders recruit from analytic, EA-adjacent ethics. Leaf is in core as a teaching programme, not a philosophy research group.
cellNotes.life|core: No ring cell in this tradition is empty or holds two or fewer entries (core 10, bridge 13, adjacent 8, potential 18), so this note covers the thin parts within each ring. In core, cybernetics has 0 entries and biology 1 (Softmax). The cybernetics zero is a real opening: the complexity notes found Equilibria Network's Viable System Model posts were the only explicit cybernetics-for-alignment work. The biology figure is also real: the Levin lab is bridge, and the biology notes found that three organisations (Softmax, Princint, ACS) carry almost all the traffic. Core also has no entry on systemic risk, security, justice, minds or meaning. That follows from the split between the two halves and is not a search miss.
cellNotes.life|bridge: Complexity has 1 bridge entry (Concordia (GDM), a DeepMind software library) and biology 2 (levin-lab, NOOMA Labs). The complexity gap is mostly real. The big complexity institutes (SFI, CSH Vienna) were checked and have no AI-risk programme, so they sit in adjacent; NECSI was not verified, so a small artefact is possible. The biology figure is probably real. Google's Paradigms of Intelligence team could not be fetched, but it would be excluded as a lab programme anyway. Neuro looks healthy with 7 entries, but most are brain-inspired AGI programmes that double as capability bets (Astera Obelisk, WBAI, BrainCog, Eon). There is no NeuroAI-for-safety fellowship, although Neuromatch's own profile says one would fit its infrastructure.
cellNotes.life|adjacent: Neuro has 0 adjacent entries and biology 1 (TWCF). The neuro zero is largely an artefact of the boundary rules. Neuroscience of what AI does to people is homed in psychology or law, with life as secondary (Sapien Labs, Winston Center (UNC), Neurorights Foundation). The same rule explains the empty Living systems × Human minds problem cell. It is partly real all the same: the neuro notes found no neuroscience or psychiatry group working on AI-induced delusion, attachment or false attribution of consciousness. The empty Living systems × Meaning cell is real but expected, since that work sits in contemplative and religious homes (Mind & Life, Human Energy).
cellNotes.life|potential: Complexity has 0 potential entries and neuro 1 (Carboncopies). The complexity zero is very probably a search artefact. The complexity angle ran only 7 web queries before the shared budget ran out, and candidates such as NECSI, IIASA's systemic-risk work, Princeton's Global Systemic Risk group and Oxford INET were never checked or failed to load. The neuro figure is part artefact, part rule. The big neuroscience funders and societies (Kavli, Simons, Allen, ASSC) were noted as having no AI-safety window but not profiled, and consciousness bodies go to AI minds. By region the tradition has nothing in Africa or MENA, and its only Latin American entry is TWCF's nominal Bahamas base. That is likely a limit of English-only search, though ALife and complexity groups in Brazil, Mexico and Chile exist and are worth a sweep.
cellNotes.indigenous|core: Empty, and this is a real opening. It should not be filled by pulling Indigenous groups into the x-risk ecosystem. 'Core' means belonging to the safety community. The Global South and non-Western sweep found no Indigenous-led or decolonial group that does, and one check search for an Indigenous-knowledge alignment fellowship found none either. The useful version is a core organisation with Indigenous co-leadership or a standing, protocol-governed partnership (see the fellowship opening), not an adjacent group relabelled as core.
cellNotes.indigenous|bridge: Only one entry, and the thinness is partly real and partly a search gap. Real: Old Ways, New is the only entry that uses safety language, and that rests on one person's role (Angie Abdilla as a reviewer of the International AI Safety Report). Search gap: the Global South and non-Western angle ran with no web searches. One search for this note turned up two 2026 leads that are not on the map: the Beyond WEIRD online conference (16 Sept 2026, with Jason Edward Lewis and Maui Hudson) and the Relational Futures project on how Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples respond to AI, including companions. The coding is also cautious. Technecultura (its founder contributed to the International AI Safety Report and sits on the advisory panel of the Global South AI Safety Report) and Masakhane (a member of the Global South Network for Trustworthy AI that plans multilingual safety benchmarks) are borderline bridges.
cellNotes.indigenous|potential: Only two entries (Local Contexts and FEL), mostly because of how the search was done, and that hides a real opening. Only minority-language bodies were swept systematically, and none of them (FPCC, First Languages Australia and others) had AI work. Indigenous data-governance and impact-assessment bodies, whose methods carry over directly, were never searched. Examples: the First Nations Information Governance Centre (OCAP principles), Maiam nayri Wingara in Australia, the US Indigenous Data Sovereignty Network, and practitioners of free, prior and informed consent. Some of these may already have AI work; I haven't checked. The one such body that was found, Local Contexts, has no AI work at all (transfer no AI work yet). The methods exist; the bridge to AI does not.
cellNotes.democracy|core: No ring cell for democracy has two or fewer entries (core 12, or 13 with Coefficient Giving; bridge 14; adjacent 37; potential 5), so this note covers the thin parts within each ring. Core leans heavily one way: 8 of 13 are forecasting/epistemics, 3 are CI tools (AOI, CIP, EIP) and only 2 are deliberation (Odyssean Institute, AI & Democracy Fdn). This looks like a real feature of the field, not a gap in the search. The collective and epistemics angles searched specifically for deliberation work framed as AI safety and found little: no dedicated funder for deliberative or pluralistic alignment, and OpenAI's Democratic Inputs was a one-off in 2023.
cellNotes.democracy|bridge: There are 14 entries, evenly split (5 tools, 4 deliberation, 5 epistemics), but fewer deliberation bridges are actually live. Habermas Machine is dormant, with no commits since Jan 2025. Global AI Dialogue is unverified, with no results since its Feb 2025 launch. The Allen Lab's GETTING-Plurality co-directorship ended in Jan 2026. That leaves roughly three active deliberation bridges: Stanford DDL, DemocracyNext and vTaiwan / g0v. This is a real opening rather than a search artefact.
cellNotes.democracy|adjacent: Adjacent is the densest ring: 37 entries, 14 of them CI-tool builders. The thin parts are geography and standpoint. Across all 69 entries there are none from Africa, Latin America or MENA, only 3 from Asia-Pacific (Taiwan, Japan, India), and 68 of 69 are tagged standpoint 'neither' (Tattle is the exception). Some of this is a search artefact, since searches were English-only. Some is probably real: the discovery notes found the Global South present only through CIP's Global Dialogues, Aapti and Build Up. The tradition also has four empty problem cells (agency, AI moral status, meaning, people). AI moral status is the one worth acting on; see openings.
cellNotes.democracy|potential: This is the thinnest cell: 5 entries (People Powered, Democracy X, Society Library, ARG-tech, Internet Archive), none of them CI tools and only 2 in deliberation. It is mostly a search artefact. None of the field's main professional deliberation practitioners appear anywhere on the map: newDemocracy Foundation, MASS LBP, Involve, Sortition Foundation, Democratic Society, Kettering Foundation and Participedia. Nor does RadicalxChange, although the discovery notes discuss it. Parliamentary technology-assessment offices were placed under arts. A targeted sweep would probably double this cell.
cellNotes.psych|core: No tradition × ring cell has two or fewer entries (6/15/38/6), so this note covers the thin parts within each ring. Core has 6 entries but is hollow. Five are field-health services (Rethink Wellbeing, Upgradable, AISS, CFAR, FABRIC / ESPR) and the sixth is UK AISI. Clinical, cognitive, developmental and relational psychology each have zero core entries. Among the five field-health entries, AISS has been dormant since July 2023, Upgradable has done little since February 2025, and CFAR has deliberately stepped back from AI framing. Part of this is a classification effect: 15 core organisations draw on psych as a secondary tradition (Eleos AI, Cambridge Digital Minds, Sophron Research, TruthfulAI, FRI, ACS Research) and are homed elsewhere. Still, no AI-safety organisation has been founded out of clinical or developmental psychology. This is a real opening.
cellNotes.psych|bridge: 15 entries, with three thin sub-cells. Relational has 1 (MIT AHA), field health 1 (MentNav) and developmental 2 (Common Sense Media, everyone.AI). The relational gap looks real. Attachment and intimacy science (Kinsey VIBES, MIT Tech & Self, AAAC) sits in adjacent or potential and describes companion harms without engaging alignment, even though UK AISI now uses the term 'socioaffective alignment'. The developmental figure is also real: only 2 of 18 developmental organisations reach bridge, and most youth work is literacy or protection.
cellNotes.psych|adjacent: 38 entries, the bulk of the tradition, of which developmental alone accounts for 15. Field health is empty by definition: support for AI-safety workers is coded core or bridge, so this is not a gap. Relational has 2 (Turkle's initiative and Kinsey), which is probably partly a search artefact. Couples and attachment research centres and the research arms of dating platforms were not swept, yet they study human-AI romantic bonding with large samples.
cellNotes.psych|potential: 6 entries, and every sub-tradition has two or fewer (clinical 1, cognitive 1, developmental 1, relational 1, social 2, field health 0). This is mostly a search artefact. The sweeps ran out of web searches, and whole professional fields leave no trace on the map: psychometrics, judgement and decision-making societies, organisational psychology (e.g. SIOP) and political psychology (e.g. ISPP). The blind-spot sweep also checked suicide-prevention and mental-health charities (Samaritans, Molly Rose Foundation, YoungMinds, IASP), found no AI work and did not list them, though they fit potential. The empty field-health cell is a real opening. Humanitarian staff-care practice and climate psychology (Climate Psych. Alliance, homed under clinical) hold transferable know-how on distress under existential stakes, with no AI bridge.
cellNotes.safety|core: The ring total (9) is above the threshold, but split by sub-tradition it is thin: public health & biosecurity has 0 core entries and safety engineering & assurance has 3. The empty health cell is partly a matter of definitions. Biosecurity groups that do frontier work (SecureBio, JHU Health Security) count as bridge because they existed before their AI work. It is also a real opening: no organisation from public health or patient safety was founded to make AI go well. Nothing like an 'AI harms epidemiology' body exists, and the blind-spot sweep found no national public-health institute that treats AI as an exposure.
