The 3 engineering cores (Gradient Institute, CLTC AI Security Init., the CAIS course) show that the system-safety community has produced almost no organisations native to AI safety. Its strongest voices, such as DASS Lab (TU Delft), stay bridge or critic. That is a real gap, not a search artefact.
cellNotes.safety|potential: The ring total is 7: 4 engineering, 1 risk (ALLFED) and 2 health (IHI Lucian Leape Inst., Deakin GLOBE). This is largely a search artefact. The safety-science sweep ran after the web-search budget was used up, and it names what it skipped: the safety-science groups at Lund, NTNU, Delft and Griffith, DNV, TÜV AI.Lab, and Japanese and Chinese assurance bodies. Nor were any of these profiled: nuclear operators' peer-review bodies (INPO, WANO), accident investigators (NTSB, AAIB, HSSIB), confidential reporting schemes (NASA ASRS, CHIRP), or process-safety bodies (CCPS, US CSB). Those hold exactly the institutional knowledge the tradition lacks on this map. Within the cell, though, the pattern is real: the leading safety-science bodies that were profiled (MIT PSASS, REA, Safer Complex Systems) have no AI programme and are tagged as doors to open.
cellNotes.contemplative|core: Two entries: Positive AI Labs (set up in 2025, nothing published yet) and Groundless (SFF recommended $16k in 2026). This is mostly a real gap: very few organisations inside the AI-safety ecosystem are founded on contemplative practice. It is partly a tagging effect. The Buddhism & AI Initiative, the only classic-map entry with a contemplative strand, is homed in religion under rule B1. Math. Metaphysics Inst. is SFF-funded but tagged bridge. Researchers inside labs who draw on contemplative ideas don't count, because the unit is the organisation. A new core organisation is worth founding only if it does tested work (see the evaluation opening), not more Convening its community.
cellNotes.contemplative|adjacent: Four entries (Mind & Life, UVA AI + Flourishing, SAND, WISR), against 23 potential. That is a hollow middle: organisations either take up an explicit alignment frame (11 bridge) or keep AI to one-off events. Part of this is a search artefact. Large contemplative-science centres such as UW-Madison's Center for Healthy Minds don't appear in the discovery notes. Asian Buddhist, Indian and Christian contemplative networks were covered thinly (the blind-spot notes list Thailand, India, and CAC and Contemplative Outreach behind Cloudflare as thin or unverified). Part is real: the discovery notes found no AI programming at about 25 retreat and contemplative centres (Omega, Spirit Rock, Upaya, Naropa, Kripalu and others), and only one AI item each at Plum Village and Oxford Mindfulness.
cellNotes.formal|adjacent: Only one entry (MCMP (LMU)). This is mostly an artefact of the taxonomy and the search, with a smaller real gap behind it. The taxonomy files formal work on AI's social effects under other traditions: fairness and accountability under law, markets and power under economics, and the metrology institutes (NPL AI Measurement, PTB AI-Met, LNE (LEIA)) under safety. The real gap is narrower. Few formal-discipline bodies use their own tools to study what AI does to their field or to society. The mathematics community's response to automated proof is the strongest candidate to fill this cell.
cellNotes.formal|potential: Seven entries, so not thin by count, but narrow. Six are statistics, decision-science or metrology societies (ASA, INFORMS DAS, DMDU Society, ENBIS, EMN Mathmet, ISBA BayesAI). The seventh is Physics of Learning. No mathematics, logic or theoretical-CS learned society appears (IMU, LMS, AMS, SIAM and SIGACT all return nothing). SIAM, IMS and INFORMS's main sites could not be read behind bot walls, so this is partly a search limit. The Simons collaboration ($2M a year, no safety framing) is the obvious way to deepen the formal core, but that core is already the best-funded part of the map. It is therefore a weaker bet for widening the field than the statistics and decision-science entries.
cellNotes.formal|bridge: Seven entries, but three of them (Topos Institute, GLAIVE, Basis) owe their AI-safety work mainly to ARIA's Safeguarded AI programme. GLAIVE has already moved to AI-for-mathematics tooling since its ARIA award closed. The bridge is real but fragile: it depends on one public funder, whose priorities narrowed to cybersecurity in 2025-26.
cellNotes.law|core: Two placed entries: AIWI and ILINA. CIFAR's CAISI programme is also core but counted as a generalist funder. Part of this is a scope choice. The aisafety.com map's own legal organisations (LawAI, CLAIR, LASST, Legal Safety Lab) come from inside the x-risk world and apply US frontier-regulation and liability law rather than an outside tradition, so they are not counted here. The opening is still real in a narrower sense. No core organisation carries human-rights law, children's-rights law, Global South legal experience or STS into safety work. Only 2 of the 93 law profiles (ILINA, AI Rights Institute) are framed around catastrophic or existential risk, and only AIWI reaches the people inside labs.
cellNotes.law|potential: Eight entries, so not strictly under the threshold, but thin for the map's largest tradition: 9% of law entries are potential, against 16% map-wide. Five are STS learned societies or history projects (EASST, 4S, CASTAC, Cambridge Histories of AI, Deutsches Museum); the others are Library Futures, the Center for Genetics and Society and the Future Generations Commissioner for Wales. This is probably a search artefact. Nobody swept law-reform commissions (the Law Commission of England and Wales, for example, published an AI discussion paper in 2025), ombudsmen, national human rights institutions other than DIHR, judicial-training bodies, access-to-justice groups, arbitration bodies, or future-generations offices outside Wales. These hold transferable methods such as liability reform, complaint handling and judicial fact-finding, and deserve one targeted sweep.
cellNotes.peace|core: Six entries. Five are diplomacy (Safe AI Forum (SAIF), Concordia AI, Oxford Martin AIGI, Simon Institute, AISA), one is arms control (UChicago XLab) and none is peacebuilding. The thin arms-control count is partly a tagging choice: IST was moved from core to bridge, yet its Recursive Self-Improvement Initiative is the only arms-control project aimed at frontier loss of control. The peacebuilding zero is a real opening. No AI-safety organisation is built on mediation or conflict transformation, and Search for Common Ground and Beyond Conflict, both on the starting list, showed no AI engagement.
cellNotes.peace|bridge: Twenty-two entries: 12 arms control and 9 diplomacy, but only 1 peacebuilding. That one is HD AI & Emerging Tech, whose state-to-state military-AI work is discreet and could not be verified after 2023. This is a real opening, not an artefact. The peacebuilders that do have AI programmes (CMI, Build Up, Toda Peace Institute, DPPA Innovation Cell) use AI in peace processes ('AI for peace'). They do not apply peace practice to AI risk, so they sit in adjacent.
cellNotes.peace|adjacent: Sixteen entries, of which only one is diplomacy (DiploFoundation). This is mostly a definitional effect rather than an opening: diplomacy bodies that take up AI usually frame it as security or catastrophic or existential risk, which puts them in bridge. It may also be partly a search artefact, because tech-diplomacy networks and foreign-ministry tech envoys were not swept systematically. Low priority.
cellNotes.peace|potential: Seven entries: four peacebuilding, two arms control (FEST Heidelberg, Geneva Academy) and one diplomacy (GESDA). Search limits are the main reason the cell is thin. This angle's web-search budget ran out after about 27 queries, and the BICC and VDW sites could not be read. The bodies with the most transferable methods were noted in the discovery notes but not profiled: verification bodies (IAEA, CTBTO, OPCW, VERTIC), negotiation-science centres (Harvard PON, Stanford SCICN), conflict-data producers (Uppsala UCDP, ACLED), and Search for Common Ground. That these hold relevant methods but do no AI work is itself the opening, so a second pass should add to this cell.

report.summary_html:
• The map holds 722 organisations across 14 traditions. Only 64 (9%) appear on the aisafety.com field map, so most of this landscape is invisible from the field's standard directory.
  • Visibility falls with distance from the sciences: 15% of Sciences & engineering entries are on the classic map, against 3% of Minds & inner life. Consciousness and AI minds has 11 core organisations and none on the classic map.
  • The biggest bodies of knowledge sit furthest from the safety frame. Law, rights & society has 91 organisations, 2 of them core and 2 framing the stakes as catastrophic. Religion has 50 and 1 core entry; Indigenous & decolonial knowledges has none.
  • Adjacent fields mostly talk to their own people: 123 of 722 organisations move their knowledge into AI models and 26 into the people who build and govern AI, while 77 of the 183 in Minds & inner life mainly convene their own community.
  • AI safety has imported the artefacts of older safety cultures (safety cases, incident databases, risk thresholds) but not their institutions: no confidential near-miss reporting, no independent accident investigation, no measurement of safety culture and no bioethics-style monitoring board was found.
  • The inner side of the field is the thinnest part of the map: 10 organisations offer direct care, one of them paused since 2023, and only 2 carry int/a's "inner work, outer change" badge.
  • Coverage leans Anglophone: 55% of entries are in North America or the UK and Ireland, and 54 are Indigenous-led or centred on the Majority World. Some of what looks empty is a limit of the search.
  • 42 openings for founders, funders and int/a follow, ranked. The first ten are flagged as places to start.

The interactive map lets you filter all 722 organisations by tradition, ring, problem, region and how to get involved. Open it here.
report.brief_html:
In October 2026, members of the int/a Europe group discussed a project worth doing: mapping the fields adjacent to AI safety, for existing and possible AI-safety work, and making them legible to existing and new funders. The prompt was a contrast. There is much talk about founding more AI-safety organisations (Coefficient Giving's Project Tailwind, a $200 million call for founders, is the latest), and little about widening the field. New funders are arriving and looking for approaches that haven't been tried.

A second point came from a conversation with the aisafety.com team, who were updating their field map. Adjacent fields weren't its focus, which is reasonable for the core, but it leaves blind spots: the field doesn't see where other disciplines already have approaches or knowledge, and risks becoming more myopic over time. The group asked for a concrete list of problems for founders and opportunities for funders, and suggested the int/a project might be the mapping itself, done as an interdisciplinary exercise. Princint (formerly PIBBSS), the Alignment of Complex Systems group and the cooperative-AI community were named as places where this kind of work already happens.

The brief points in a direction rather than fixing a scope, so four decisions shaped this report.

  • The unit is the organisation. Labs, nonprofits, programmes, funders, networks, professional bodies and companies, not essays or individuals. The essays and talks in the seed list appear as the key work of the organisations behind them.
  • "AI going well" is read broadly. Many adjacent fields don't use the language of existential risk, and excluding them would reproduce the blind spot. The rings keep the difference visible: an organisation's distance from the AI-safety core is shown, not hidden.
  • The main axis is the adjacent field. Each organisation is placed by the tradition of knowledge it brings, which is what the brief asked to make legible. What it works on is a second, independent axis, so the two can be crossed to find empty niches.
  • Possible work counts too. The brief mentions possible as well as existing AI-safety work, so the map includes potential partners: organisations whose knowledge is plainly relevant but which have barely engaged with AI. These are the doors a founder or funder would have to open.
report.organised_html:
Every organisation is tagged on a handful of facets, each answering one question a reader might ask. The categories were designed by four independent designers working from different starting points (by discipline, by problem, through int/a's integral frames, and by what each kind of reader needs to find), scored by two judges with opposite priorities (a sceptical funder and map editor; an int/a steward and interdisciplinary facilitator), and merged by a synthesiser. The definitions are in the map's Guide tab.

Tradition: what it brings. Fourteen traditions, grouped into four families. Sciences & engineering: safety and risk sciences; formal and physical sciences; life and systems sciences. Minds & inner life: consciousness and AI minds; psychology and cognitive science; contemplative and integral traditions; religion and theology. Humanities & cultures: philosophy and ethics; arts, narrative and futures; Indigenous and decolonial knowledges. Society & institutions: law, rights and society; economics, labour and commons; democracy and collective intelligence; peace, security and diplomacy. Each organisation has one home tradition and up to two others it draws on substantially.

Ring: how close it is to the AI-safety core. Core, bridge, adjacent and potential, as defined above. A ring is a statement about proximity, not worth: much of the most interesting work on this map sits in the outer rings.

Problem: what it works on. Fourteen problems in four areas. The AI itself: understanding AI and agency; what AI should value; assurance and oversight; the moral status of AI. Human minds & meaning: protecting minds and relationships; meaning, dignity and formation; the people doing the work. Living & deciding together: sensemaking, truth and foresight; democratic voice and legitimacy; rights and plural voices; power, wealth and work. Cooperation, conflict & civilisation: multi-agent AI and cooperation; security and international coordination; systemic risk and the metacrisis.

Lenses. A few further facets are there to see the field differently. What flows where asks who or what changes because of the work: the AI models, the people who build and govern them, institutions, or mainly the organisation's own community. The integral quadrant asks whether the work attends to inner experience (I), shared meaning (We), mechanisms (It) or collective systems (Its). What is at stake records how the organisation itself frames the stakes. Way of knowing records what kind of knowledge its main output is, from formal proof to contemplative practice to communal and lived knowledge. Sparse int/a badges mark clear exemplars of one of int/a's five principles. Practical facets cover what the organisation does, how to get involved, type, region, status and nearness to int/a's hubs.
report.findings_html:
1. Most of the wider field is invisible from the standard map. Of 722 organisations, 64 are on the aisafety.com field map. None of the 28 consciousness and AI-minds organisations is there although 11 are core, and neither is any of the 40 contemplative or 15 Indigenous & decolonial entries. The classic map is a good guide to the core; it is not a guide to the knowledge around it.
  2. AI safety has absorbed formal science and little else. The formal and physical sciences are the one tradition the field already owns: 17 of 32 organisations are core, 12 are on the classic map and only 1 is adjacent. Much of the new money of 2025 and 2026 has gone to mathematics, learning theory and verification, for example Coefficient Giving's $10 million to the new Mathematical AI Safety Institute and ARIA's £59 million Safeguarded AI programme.
  3. The largest knowledge bases are furthest out. The adjacent ring is the largest, with 320 organisations. Law (91), democracy and collective intelligence (68), psychology (65) and economics (60) are the biggest traditions, and all of them sit mostly outside the safety frame. Their methods (litigation, assemblies, clinical evidence, antitrust and supervision) are tested at scale but rarely applied to frontier AI.
  4. Knowledge rarely reaches the builders. Only 26 organisations change the people who build, govern and fund AI, against 123 that work on the models and many more that inform institutions or convene their own community. Psychology studies users and children; nobody on the map studies the psychology of the labs and governments steering AI.
  5. Artefacts without institutions. The safety and risk sciences have 67 organisations on the map, 3 of them on the classic map. Frontier AI has taken their safety cases, risk thresholds and incident databases, but not confidential near-miss reporting, independent investigation, just culture or peer review. Philosophy shows the same split: AI safety adopted its theories of value, while 17 of the 18 applied-ethics and bioethics bodies, which hold fifty years of oversight practice, sit in the adjacent ring.
  6. Two communities study the same people from opposite sides. 27 of the 28 consciousness organisations work on AI moral status; 47 of the 65 psychology organisations work on protecting human minds, and none on moral status. Both study people who come to believe an AI is conscious, the welfare researchers to take the belief seriously and the clinicians to treat its harms, and they do not work together.
  7. int/a's own milieu is mostly potential. 22 of the 40 contemplative and integral organisations (55%) are potential partners, the highest share of any tradition, and only 2 are core. The contemplative world's funders make no AI grants, and the groups turning contemplative insight into alignment proposals have not yet tested them against the safety field's own evaluations.
  8. Religion has reach, and a shallow bridge. The 50 religious organisations include norm-setters that speak for billions and have already issued AI rulings (the Holy See's Magnifica Humanitas, the International Islamic Fiqh Academy's Resolution 258, ICESCO's Riyadh Charter), but none of those rulings addresses loss of control. The main bridge to AI safety is a single round of FLI grants to faith communities (16 grants, about $1.36 million).
  9. Democracy's forecasting strand made it in; its legitimacy strand didn't. 6 of the 9 democracy and collective-intelligence organisations on the classic map are forecasting or epistemics groups. Assemblies, deliberative polling and consensus conferences, the tradition's machinery of legitimacy, have not reached the decisions the safety field cares most about, such as capability thresholds, pauses or AI moral status.
  10. Multi-agent risk is thinly staffed across traditions. Only 36 organisations work on populations of interacting AI agents. Economics has 2 of 60; peace has none, though conflict between parties is its core subject; collective-behaviour biologists and evolutionary game theorists sit in the potential ring. The disciplines that study cooperation and conflict among many agents are mostly not yet looking at AI agents.

Parallel worlds

Several problems on the map are worked on by two or more communities that barely know each other. Power concentration is the clearest. Inside the safety field, Formation Research, Longview's power-concentration call, the Alignment of Complex Systems group's work on gradual disempowerment and the Post-AGI workshops treat it as a structural risk from advanced AI. Outside it, the Open Markets Institute, the AI Now Institute, MIT's Stone Center, the unions (the TUC, UTAW and Unite at Google DeepMind, the Alphabet Workers Union) and the financial-stability supervisors work on the same concentration with antitrust law, collective bargaining and macroprudential tools. The two sides cite different literatures and meet at different conferences.

The same split runs through human minds. The UK AI Security Institute's societal-resilience team and the AI-welfare groups study persuasion, sycophancy and attribution of mind from the model's side; psychiatrists at King's College London, Aarhus and Beth Israel Deaconess, the psychoanalysts' AI commission, BACP and the child-development groups (Common Sense Media, Fairplay, 5Rights) study the same harms from the person's side. Among consciousness researchers, 27 of 28 work on AI moral status, while 47 of 65 psychology organisations work on protecting minds and none works on moral status, although both study people who come to believe an AI is conscious.

Law repeats the pattern: the x-risk legal groups on the classic map have little contact with the 91 rights, liability and accountability organisations, of which only 2 frame the stakes as catastrophic. Democracy splits between its forecasting strand, which the safety field has adopted (6 of the tradition's 9 classic-map entries are forecasting or epistemics groups), and its legitimacy strand of assemblies and deliberation, which it has not. Peace splits between arms control and Track II diplomacy, which work on AI, and peacebuilding and mediation, which mostly do not.

Connecting these worlds would yield more than goodwill. Each side holds something the other lacks: evaluation methods and threat models on one side, clinical evidence, legal remedies, institutional legitimacy and decades of practice on the other. Several openings below are bridges of exactly this kind: shared evaluations built with clinicians, translation fellowships, joint research agendas and convenings with a fixed output.

The people doing the work

The people who build, govern, fund and research AI are the least served part of this map. Only 10 organisations offer direct care or support to individuals, and they are fragile: AI Safety Support has been paused since July 2023, Upgradable has done little since early 2025, Mental Health Navigator runs on about £1,200 a year, and Rethink Wellbeing is not specific to AI. The AI Whistleblower Initiative supports insiders who raise concerns, and the Data Labelers Association and the Data Workers' Inquiry speak for the workforce that produces safety-relevant labels.

The need is documented. The seed list cites a 2026 write-up of survey data reporting burnout among 59% of AI-safety respondents, and forum posts describe stress that cannot be taken to an outside therapist because of non-disclosure agreements, anticipatory grief about the future, and isolation outside the main hubs. Psychology on this map studies users, children and patients far more than it studies the people and institutions steering AI: no organisation measures safety culture inside labs or studies how decision-makers perceive the race.

Other fields already know how to do much of this. Humanitarian organisations have staff-care guidelines for people exposed to distressing material; governments have clinicians cleared to hear classified material; climate psychology runs groups for distress about the future; chaplaincy has codified ethics of presence and referral; medicine and engineering have professional oaths and just-culture reporting. None of these has been adapted for AI.

Any support offered to AI people needs safeguards from the start. The most visible contemplative programme for technologists, MAPLE, faces serious, detailed public allegations of high-control dynamics, contested by its supporters. Independent governance, clear complaint routes, no discouraging of outside therapy, and norms on sleep, money and hierarchy are the minimum, and the openings below build them in.
report.openings_intro_html: Eighteen analysts, one for each tradition and four for cross-cutting questions, read the profiles and statistics and proposed 52 openings. Five of the eighteen and the final synthesiser did not complete their work, so the selection, merging and ranking below, the arts note and the cross-cutting essays were done in the main session. Each opening names the part of the map it would fill and who is nearby. They were not individually tested against the open web; ten of the strongest were spot-checked for prior work, and one was narrowed as a result. Treat each as a well-grounded hypothesis to check before acting.
report.atlas_intro_html: Organisations are grouped by their home tradition and, within it, by ring. Each entry gives what the organisation is, why it matters for this map, what it works on, its key work and how to get involved. Badges mark entries already on the aisafety.com map and any status worth knowing. Every entry is also in the interactive map, where it can be filtered and compared.
report.funders_intro_html:
Money for this wider field comes from three groups that rarely fund together. The AI-safety funders (the Survival and Flourishing Fund, Coefficient Giving, the Future of Life Institute, Macroscopic Ventures, Longview and the Navigation Fund) fund almost entirely in the core and bridge rings, and mostly in the formal and life sciences, consciousness and AI welfare, and forecasting. Public research money for AI safety, such as ARIA's £59 million Safeguarded AI programme and the £27 million Alignment Project led by the UK AI Security Institute, follows similar lines with a stronger pull towards mathematics and verification.

The second group funds the adjacent ring and frames AI as present harm or public interest. Humanity AI has committed $500 million over five years from ten foundations, Current AI reports $404 million pledged for public-interest AI, Omidyar Network, Mozilla and the European AI & Society Fund back rights and accountability groups, and Anthropic's Economic Futures programme has a $200 million research fund. These funders reach the law, economics and democracy traditions that hold most of the map's organisations, but rarely the questions about the AI itself.

The third group funds the traditions this map is about without any AI-safety framing. Templeton World Charity Foundation put about $2.8 million into three Diverse Intelligences hubs in 2025, and the John Templeton Foundation's Future of Intelligence venture will give more than $60 million over 2026 to 2028. Lilly Endowment gave $50.8 million to Notre Dame's DELTA network for faith-based formation in an age of AI. Lloyd's Register Foundation (a £300 million grant portfolio, with £13.9 million to York's Centre for Assuring Autonomy) and UL Research Institutes fund engineering safety, and Carnegie Corporation funds the AI-and-nuclear work of the peace tradition.

Some traditions have no dedicated funder for AI work at all. The contemplative world's grant-makers (Fetzer, Kalliopeia, 1440, Hemera, Templeton Religion Trust) were found to make no AI grants, which helps explain why 22 of the 40 contemplative organisations sit in the potential ring. No AI-safety funder backs any of the Indigenous-led organisations, and the psychological support services for the field's own workers run on very little.

The most promising moves for funders are co-funding pairs that cross these groups: a safety funder with Templeton on comparative cognition and consciousness science; with Lloyd's Register Foundation or UL Research Institutes on placing system-safety engineers; with Carnegie Corporation on verification expertise; with Mind & Life and the contemplative funders on a contemplative-science call; and with faith funders on carrying frontier-risk concerns into religious norm-setting. The newest and largest funder of all, the OpenAI Foundation, holds a stake in OpenAI worth more than $100 billion, and where it chooses to sit among these groups will matter more than any single grant.
report.inta_html:
The map says something specific about int/a's own milieu. Contemplative and integral organisations number 40, and 22 of them are potential partners with little or no AI work; only 2 sit in the core. The int/a principle badges were given sparingly, and only 2 organisations carry the "inner work, outer change" badge: integral altruism itself and Connecting Intelligence. The traditions int/a draws on hold a great deal of relevant knowledge and very few bridges to where AI is being built and governed.

That points to a role suited to a volunteer community with hubs in London (66 organisations on the map are active there), Paris (28) and Berlin (25). int/a can translate: write the briefs that restate AI-safety problems in the language of contemplative science, faith traditions or bioethics, and carry them to the people who can act. It can convene where pace and trust matter, such as dialogues between AI-safety and AI-ethics researchers, or workshops joining clinicians and consciousness researchers, in the spirit of moving at the speed of wisdom. And it can model care for the people doing the work, with the safeguards that the MAPLE allegations show are needed.

The suggestion in the brief that the mapping itself could be the int/a project is the strongest of all. This map was made quickly by AI agents; a version corrected tradition by tradition by practitioners would be more accurate, and the process would build the relationships the openings depend on. A post per tradition for the int/a Substack or the EA Forum, and a one-page brief for funders, would make the work legible to new funders, which was the original aim.

Two cautions. The integral and contemplative world has its own failure modes, from guru dynamics to grand theory without evidence, and int/a's credibility with funders depends on holding its own proposals to the same tests it asks of others: the contemplative self-preservation study and the wisdom benchmark below are designed to produce publishable null results as readily as positive ones. And the map should not become a way of claiming the field's adjacent traditions for int/a: most of these organisations have never heard of it, and the first step is listening to them.

Openings marked for int/a in the list above are ones a volunteer community with hubs in London, Berlin and Paris could take on directly.
report.method_html:
How it was made

  1. Seeds and baseline. The user's initial search (64 items, mostly essays and talks) and the aisafety.com field map, whose 343 named entries were read on 4 October 2026 to mark which organisations it already lists.
  2. Discovery. Eighteen research agents each swept one adjacent field or angle, a completeness critic named the blind spots, and seven more agents searched them: 596 candidates. Duplicates were merged and out-of-scope entries dropped (552). A second sweep then covered disciplines, faiths and regions still missing (education, anthropology, linguistics, libraries and archives, audit and actuarial science, statistics, epidemiology, under-covered faith traditions, continental Europe, Asia and Latin America), adding 171.
  3. Categories. Four independent designs, two judges and a synthesiser produced the facets described above.
  4. Profiles. Each organisation was researched on its own site and at least one other source by an agent writing seven profiles at a time, then tagged against the taxonomy's written rules.
  5. Fact-check. A second, adversarial agent re-checked each batch: URL, status, founding date, place, people, funding, key work, ring and tags. Of 722 profiles checked, 268 were corrected and 0 rejected. Corrections were mostly to people, summaries, caveats, dates and funding; tags changed rarely.
  6. Reliability. Two further coders re-tagged a stratified sample of 83 organisations without seeing the original tags. They agreed with each other on the home tradition 99% of the time (Cohen's kappa 0.99) and on the ring 95% (kappa 0.93); against the original tags, the ring matched 88% of the time. How an organisation frames the stakes agreed least (kappa 0.73 against the original). All coders were the same kind of AI agent reading the same descriptions, so these figures show that the rules are applied consistently, not that they are right.
  7. Openings. Eighteen analysts were asked to propose openings from the profiles and statistics: one per tradition, and four on cross-cutting questions (funders, bridges between parallel communities, int/a's role, the people doing the work). Thirteen completed and proposed 52 openings. The other five, and the final synthesiser, stopped without doing the work, so the selection, merging and ranking into the 42 shown here, the note on arts and the cross-cutting essays were written in the main session from the same data. Openings were not individually tested against the open web; ten of the strongest were spot-checked for prior work, and one was narrowed.

Limits

  • This was made by AI research agents, reviewed and assembled by one more. Errors are likely in individual entries, especially in dates, people and funding. Each entry links its sources; check them before relying on a detail.
  • Web search ran out early. The research agents shared a limited web-search budget, which was spent during the first discovery sweep. Later discovery and most fact-checking worked by reading organisations' own sites and known sources directly. That is reliable for what an organisation says it does, weaker for recent news it hasn't published, and weakest for finding organisations nobody already knew of.
  • Sector sizes are not field sizes. Some traditions had dedicated sweeps (religion, labour, futures, membership bodies), others didn't. Coverage is skewed to English-language and online-visible work: 55% of entries are based in North America or the UK and Ireland. Non-English Europe, Asia, Africa and Latin America are certainly under-represented.
  • Searched and found nothing. No organisation engaging AI was found among Hindu, Sikh, Jain, Shinto, Daoist or Benedictine bodies, among the national public-health institutes checked, among forensic-linguistics groups, or among structured-expert-judgement communities. No organisation does ethnography of AI labs or keeps an archive of the AI-safety field's history. Some of these are real gaps and some are limits of the search; the tradition notes say which where it is known.
  • Rings and tags are judgements. The rules are written down and applied consistently, but reasonable people will place some organisations differently. Inclusion is not endorsement. Where an organisation faces serious public criticism, as with MAPLE, its entry says so.
  • Statuses go stale. Everything here reflects what was findable in early October 2026.
